newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin says he would agree to second term.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin says he would agree to second term.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Wednesday he would agree to serve a second term as finance minister, assuming his government is re-elected and he is asked to fill the post by the prime minister.
Martin also said he favors setting debt-to-gross domestic product targets for the country following a public debate on the proper level for such a target.
"If the prime minister were to offer me the job in the next mandate I would most certainly accept it," Martin told a Nesbitt Burns telephone conference.

Martin said he believes setting a debt-to-GDP ratio target is something the country should be aiming for in the long run. While he would not specify what he thought the target should be, Martin said he thought a target of 60 percent was not ambitious enough. He noted the ratio was once 20 percent and said the ideal level may now lie between 20 and 60 percent.

Martin said reducing taxes is a priority for his government, but it is too soon to declare victory in the battle to reduce the deficit. Martin also said the government will not cut taxes if such a cut would leave it unable to finance social programs.

"Our major goal here, as quickly as we can do it responsibly, is to see taxes come down," said Martin. "We're going to do it, I can tell you, in a way that will not jeopardize the very hard won fiscal gains that we have so far."
Martin said he does not favor balanced budget legislation because he did not believe it would be effective.
Setting targets for the unemployment rate would also be ineffective, he said, adding that Canada should now begin to see a gradual long-term decline in the jobless rate.
Martin again pledged to keep inflation low.
"We are not going to let inflationary pressures ever get out of hand in this country again. The cost of having to quench inflation is simply too great," said Martin.
